prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I shall never get you put together entirely, Pieced, glued, and properly jointed. Mule-bray, pig-grunt and bawdy cackles Proceed from your great lips. It’s worse than a barnyard. Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle, Mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other. Thirty years now I have labored To dredge the silt from your throat. I am none the wiser. Scaling little ladders with glue pots and pails of lysol I crawl like an ant in mourning Over the weedy acres of your brow To mend the immense skull plates and clear The bald, white tumuli of your eyes. A blue sky out of the Oresteia Arches above us. O father, all by yourself You are pithy and historical as the Roman Forum. I open my lunch on a hill of black cypress. Your fluted bones and acanthine hair are littered In their old anarchy to the horizon-line. It would take more than a lightning-stroke To create such a ruin. Nights, I squat in the cornucopia Of your left ear, out of the wind, Counting the red stars and those of plum-color. The sun rises under the pillar of your tongue. My hours are married to shadow. No longer do I listen for the scrape of a keel On the blank stones of the landing.

I shall never put you together entirely—  
pieced, glued, and properly jointed.

outputs.L2:
I will never manage to restore you to wholeness, no matter how carefully I fit, fasten, and seal your fragments. From your enormous mouth come the sounds of a donkey, a hog, and indecent laughter—a din more dreadful than any farmyard. Maybe you imagine you are a prophet, speaking on behalf of the dead or some nameless deity. For three decades I have worked to clear the sediment choking your voice, yet I understand no more than before.

Carrying adhesive and disinfectant up tiny ladders, I move like a grieving insect across the overgrown expanse of your forehead. I try to repair the vast sections of your shattered cranium and clean the smooth, pale burial mounds that form your eyes. Above us stretches a blue heaven worthy of the *Oresteia*.

Father, even in isolation you possess the compressed weight of history, like the ruins of the Roman Forum. I unpack my meal on a mound covered with dark cypress trees. Your grooved bones and foliage-shaped hair lie scattered in ancient disorder as far as the horizon. No single bolt of lightning could have produced devastation on this scale.

At night I shelter from the wind inside the hornlike curve of your left ear, crouching there while I count stars colored crimson and deep purple. Dawn appears beneath the column of your tongue. My life has become bound to darkness. I have stopped waiting to hear a ship’s hull grate against the bare stones of the shore.
outputs.L3: The speaker struggles in vain to reconstruct a colossal but ruined father figure whose fragmented presence dominates her life. His voice is described through crude and chaotic sounds, suggesting something potentially prophetic or oracular, yet it yields no coherent message or useful wisdom. For thirty years, the speaker has mournfully devoted herself to understanding his legacy, cleansing and repairing his broken remains as though patient labor might restore both the father and her connection to him. Through classical imagery, he is transformed into an immense historical ruin—an ancient statue whose shattered body forms the landscape of the speaker’s world. She lives within his shadow, bound to grief, memory, and the impossible task of reconstruction. By the end, however, she no longer expects his return: hope has given way to resignation, and the father remains a vast but irrecoverable presence.
outputs.L4:
In Sylvia Plath’s “The Colossus,” the speaker presents her relationship with her dead or absent father as an endless archaeological task. He appears not as an ordinary human being but as a gigantic shattered statue whose fragments dominate the landscape. The speaker devotes herself to piecing him together, cleaning the ruins, and trying to recover meaning from his broken speech. Equipped with ladders, tools, and glue, she resembles both an archaeologist restoring an ancient monument and a dutiful daughter attempting to reconstruct a parent from incomplete memories.

The imagery of classical antiquity emphasizes the father’s overwhelming authority. References to ruined sculpture, Roman forums, tragic drama, and monumental architecture elevate him into a figure of almost mythical importance. At the same time, this grandeur is repeatedly undermined. The sounds that emerge from him are confused and animal-like rather than wise or prophetic, while his enormous body has become weathered, fragmented, and overgrown. He is therefore both powerful and powerless: physically ruined and incapable of answering the speaker, yet still large enough to shape her entire emotional world.

The speaker’s labor is painstaking but futile. For thirty years she has tried to clear away the accumulated debris that blocks his voice, but she remains “none the wiser.” Her work cannot restore him to life or produce a final explanation of who he was. Instead, she inhabits his ruins, sheltered and confined by them. The father’s broken body becomes the landscape of her existence, suggesting that grief has absorbed her identity and limited her ability to imagine a life beyond him.

By the poem’s conclusion, the speaker no longer expects rescue or revelation. She has stopped listening for the arrival of a ship that might carry her away, implying resignation rather than resolution. The past cannot be fully recovered, and the father cannot be reconstructed into a coherent, comprehensible whole. Yet his absence remains monumental. Plath thus portrays paternal loss as a force that persists precisely because it cannot be repaired: the father is gone, but his shadow continues to govern the daughter’s inner life.
outputs.L5: Mara **pieced** together the torn map, tracing a narrow path through the mountains. She loaded her supplies onto a stubborn **mule** and checked the darkening sky. The journey would be difficult, but turning back was not an option. Taking a deep breath, she whispered, “**Proceed**,” and led the mule toward the distant pass.
